title: Isothermal Process
short_intro: An isothermal process is a thermodynamic process in which the temperature of a system remains constant, maintained by thermal contact with a heat reservoir. During this process, internal energy remains constant for an ideal gas, and all heat added is completely converted into work.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition, Boyle's law verification, P-V characteristics, work done calculation for an ideal gas, and basic isothermal expansion or compression problems.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Advanced derivation of isothermal work done, isothermal elasticity, slope of isothermal curve on P-V diagrams compared to adiabatic curves, and deviation of real gases from isothermal behavior.

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Thermal Equilibrium
bullets: The system temperature remains strictly constant throughout the process (dT = 0).
Achieved practically by keeping the system in contact with a large heat reservoir (constant temperature bath) and allowing very slow (quasi-static) changes.
For an ideal gas, internal energy depends solely on temperature, hence change in internal energy (dU = 0).

concept_notes.heading: Equation of State (Boyle's Law)
bullets: Derived from the ideal gas equation PV = nRT when T is constant.
Yields PV = constant, meaning pressure is inversely proportional to volume.
Represents a rectangular hyperbola on a P-V (Indicator) diagram.

concept_notes.heading: Work Done in an Isothermal Process
bullets: Since temperature is constant, work done is entirely at the expense of heat supplied to the system (Q = W).
Calculated by integrating the pressure-volume function along the isothermal path from initial volume V<sub>1</sub> to final volume V<sub>2</sub>.
Can be expressed in terms of pressures as P<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> ln(P<sub>1</sub> / P<sub>2</sub>).

concept_notes.heading: Isothermal Elasticity
bullets: Defined as the ratio of stress to volumetric strain under constant temperature conditions.
Mathematically equal to the operating pressure P of the gas.
Differs from adiabatic elasticity, which is given by gamma P.

derivations.title: Work Done During Isothermal Expansion/Compression
derivations.conditions: n moles of an ideal gas undergoing a reversible isothermal process from (P_1, V_1) to (P_2, V_2) at temperature T.
steps: Start from the definition of mechanical work: W = \int_{V_1}^{V_2} P dV.
Substitute pressure from the ideal gas equation: P = \frac{nRT}{V}.
Factor out constant terms: W = nRT \int_{V_1}^{V_2} \frac{1}{V} dV.
Apply Boyle's law substitution to express in pressures if required: \frac{V_2}{V_1} = \frac{P_1}{P_2}.

derivations.title: Slope of the Isothermal Curve on a P-V Diagram
derivations.conditions: Ideal gas undergoing an isothermal process where PV = constant.
steps: Write the equation for the isothermal curve: PV = C (where C is constant).
Differentiate both sides with respect to V: P dV + V dP = 0.
Rearrange to solve for the derivative dP/dV: V dP = -P dV.

graphs_and_experiments.title: P-V Indicator Diagram for Isothermal Process
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A downward-sloping rectangular hyperbola curve on a P-V graph, showing pressure decreasing as volume increases.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Represents Boyle's law; different curves (isotherms) at different temperatures lie higher for higher temperatures (T_2 > T_1).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested in identifying isothermal vs. adiabatic curves (isotherm is less steep than adiabat).

graphs_and_experiments.title: P-T and V-T Diagrams for Isothermal Process
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line parallel to the pressure axis on a T-P graph, and a straight line parallel to the volume axis on a T-V graph.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Explicitly highlights that temperature remains constant regardless of variations in pressure or volume.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in objective questions to test graph recognition for thermodynamic processes.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Clément and Desormes' Apparatus Principle
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic setup of a large glass flask with a wide mouth, stopcock, manometer, and pressure pump.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Used to determine the ratio of specific heats (gamma) by combining slow (isothermal) and rapid (adiabatic) operations.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual questions on experimental verification of thermodynamic constants in PGT physics.

solved_numericals.question: 2 moles of an ideal gas expand isothermally at 300 K from an initial volume of 20 litres to 60 litres. Calculate the work done by the gas. (R = 8.314 J mol^-1 K^-1, \ln 3 = 1.0986)
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: n = 2 mol, T = 300 K, V_1 = 20 L, V_2 = 60 L, R = 8.314 J/(mol K).
Use the isothermal work formula: W = nRT \ln(V_2 / V_1).

solved_numericals.question: An ideal gas at 27 °C is compressed isothermally to one-fourth of its initial volume. If the initial pressure is 100 kPa, find the final pressure and the total heat released by the gas per mole.
solution_steps: Find final pressure using Boyle's law: P_1 V_1 = P_2 V_2, where V_2 = V_1 / 4. Thus, P_2 = 4 P_1.
Use the first law of thermodynamics: Q = W = nRT \ln(V_2 / V_1) for 1 mole (n = 1).
Compute value: Q = - 2494.2 \times 1.386 = - 3456.9 \text{ J} (negative sign indicates heat released).
solved_numericals.answer: Final pressure = 400 kPa; Heat released = 3456.9 J

solved_numericals.question: Compare the slope of an isothermal curve with that of an adiabatic curve for an ideal gas at a given state (P, V). Given the adiabatic exponent is \gamma.
solution_steps: Recall the adiabatic curve relation: PV^\gamma = \text{constant}.
Differentiate implicitly: P \gamma V^{\gamma-1} dV + V^\gamma dP = 0.
Take the ratio of adiabatic slope to isothermal slope: \frac{\text{Slope}_{\text{ad}}}{\text{Slope}_{\text{iso}}} = \gamma.
solved_numericals.answer: The adiabatic curve is \gamma times steeper than the isothermal curve.

assumptions_and_limitations.assumption: The process occurs quasi-statically, meaning it proceeds infinitesimally slowly to maintain continuous thermal equilibrium with the surroundings.
assumptions_and_limitations.limitation: Real-world gas expansions or compressions happen at finite speeds, introducing non-equilibrium thermal gradients and viscous losses.

assumptions_and_limitations.assumption: The working substance strictly obeys the ideal gas equation PV = nRT.
assumptions_and_limitations.limitation: Real gases deviate significantly from ideal behavior at high pressures and low temperatures due to intermolecular forces and finite molecular volumes.

common_misconceptions.wrong: An isothermal process means the container must be insulated.
common_misconceptions.correct: An isothermal process requires a highly conducting container in contact with a constant temperature heat reservoir.
common_misconceptions.why: Insulation prevents heat exchange, leading instead to an adiabatic process.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Since temperature is constant, no heat flows into or out of the system.
common_misconceptions.correct: Heat flows freely to maintain constant temperature when work is done.
common_misconceptions.why: By the First Law, Q = W; if a gas expands isothermally, it must absorb heat from the reservoir to keep its temperature from falling.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The isothermal slope is steeper than the adiabatic slope on a P-V diagram.
common_misconceptions.correct: The adiabatic curve is steeper by a factor of gamma.
common_misconceptions.why: Gamma (>1) multiplies the pressure term in the adiabatic derivative, making its absolute slope larger.

quick_revision: Isothermal process implies dT = 0 and delta U = 0 for an ideal gas.
Governed by Boyle's Law: PV = constant.
Work done during isothermal expansion/compression is W = nRT ln(V_2 / V_1).
Molar heat capacity in an isothermal process is infinite (C = infinity).
Isothermal elasticity equals the current pressure (E_T = P).
On a P-V indicator diagram, isotherms are rectangular hyperbolas.
